q-103539.name: Question 1
q-103539.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{2}$ at the point $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{4}).$
q-103539.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{2}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{4{x}^{2}}+\frac{x}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(-\frac{1}{2}),$ which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-\frac{1}{2})=-\frac{1}{2}\cdot {(-\frac{1}{2})}^{-3}+\frac{1}{2}=\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{2}{9}.
$$

q-71526.name: Question 2
q-71526.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=2{x}^{3}-7x$ at the point $(-1,5).$
q-71526.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-7x.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}-7x)=6{x}^{2}-7\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(-1,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(-1)=6(-1)^{2}-7=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-1)}=1.
$$

q-103531.name: Question 3
q-103531.problem: Find the slope of the normal line to the curve $y=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}$ at the point $(1,0).$
q-103531.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}.$ Computing the derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3/2}-2{x}^{2}) \\  & =3{x}^{1/2}-4x.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute ${f}^{′}(1)$, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{1/2}-4(1)=-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=1.
$$

q-342153.name: Question 4
q-342153.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=4-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4-{x}^{-1/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(\frac{1}{4},2):$

$$
m={f}^{′}(\frac{1}{4})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{3}}}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{(\frac{1}{4})}^{3}}}=4
$$

Therefore, the slope ${m}^{′}$ of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{′} & =-\frac{1}{m} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,9):$

$$
m={f}^{′}(2)=4(2)=8

q-47412.name: Question 6
q-47412.problem: The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}$ at the point $(1,3)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p-q.$
q-47412.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{3}{{x}^{3}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{-3}) \\  & =-9{x}^{-4} \\  & =-\frac{9}{{x}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(1)=-\frac{9}{(1)^{4}}=-9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=\frac{1}{9}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(3) & =\frac{1}{9}(x-1) \\ 9y-27 & =x-1 \\ x-9y & =-26.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p-q=-9-(-26)=17.$

q-47412.html:
Question 6
?

The equation of the normal line to the curve y=3x3 at the point (1,3) is given by x+py=q where p and q are constants. Find the value of p−q.

a
−17
b
35
c
20
d
−35
e
17
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let f(x)=3x3. First, we compute the derivative: f′(x)=ddx(3x3)=ddx(3x−3)=−9x−4=−9x4

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point (1,3): m=f′(1)=−9(1)4=−9

Therefore, the slope of the normal line m′ is m′=−1m=19.

Finally, the equation of the normal line is y−(3)=19(x−1)9y−27=x−1x−9y=−26.

Therefore, p−q=−9−(−26)=17.

q-104073.name: Question 7
q-104073.problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}$ at the point $(8,12)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
q-104073.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2/3}) \\  & =2{x}^{-1/3} \\  & =\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(8)=\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{8}}=1,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-12 & =-(x-8) \\ y & =-x+8+12 \\ y & =20-x.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =20-0 \\ y & =20.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,20).$

q-104073.html:
Question 7
?

Find where the normal line to the curve f(x)=3x23 at the point (8,12) intersects the y-axis.

a
 (0,−8)
b
 (0,−20)
c
 (0,−4)
d
 (0,4)
e
 (0,20)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Taking the derivative, we have f′(x)=ddx(3x23)=ddx(3x2/3)=2x−1/3=2x3.

So the slope of the tangent line is m=f′(8)=283=1, and therefore the slope of the normal line is m′=−1m=−1.

Finally, the equation of the normal line is y−12=−(x−8)y=−x+8+12y=20−x.

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the y-axis by setting x=0 and solving the resulting equation. We get y=20−0y=20.

Therefore, the normal line intersects the y-axis at (0,20).

q-308821.name: Question 8
q-308821.problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y={x}^{3}$ at the point $(1,1)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at
$($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $).$
q-308821.worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})=3{x}^{2}.
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=3(1)^{2}=3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-\frac{1}{3}(x-(1)) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{1}{3}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}x+\frac{4}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{4}{3} \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(\,4,0\,).$
